name: Title 1
text:
Enhancing Software Evolution Reliability
through Neurosymbolic Reasoning
textPreview: Enhancing Software Evolution Reliability | through Neurosymbolic Reasoning

name: Subtitle 2
text:
Xiufeng Xu
PhD Thesis Defense · Nanyang Technological University
Supervisor: Prof. Yi Li · 2026
textPreview: Xiufeng Xu | PhD Thesis Defense · Nanyang Technological University | Supervisor: Prof. Yi Li · 2026

text:
Good morning, and thank you for being here. My name is Xiufeng Xu, and today I will present my doctoral research, entitled “Enhancing Software Evolution Reliability through Neurosymbolic Reasoning.”

I would like to begin with a very small software change: changing one version number in a dependency file. A one-line dependency change can alter library behavior and break a downstream client. Repairing such failures then raises two further lifecycle challenges: locating the relevant logic across an unfamiliar repository and keeping delivered documentation consistent with evolved behavior.

These related challenges motivate my thesis. My central argument is that the flexibility of large language models is valuable, but reliable software evolution also requires reproducible evidence and formal, verifiable reasoning.

[Timing] 0:00–0:50

[Sources]
- Xiufeng Xu, PhD thesis, title page and Abstract, 2026.
- Thesis.cls, document variables for title, author, degree, institution, and supervisor.

textPreview: THESIS / MOTIVATION | One-line changes ripple across dependencies

name: Footer Placeholder 3
text: College of Computing and Data Science
textPreview: College of Computing and Data Science

text:
Software is almost never built once and then left unchanged. A useful system must continuously adapt to new requirements, new platforms, security threats, defects, and changing dependencies. This continuous process is software evolution.

The difficulty is that modern software is not an isolated program. It is a node in a large dependency network. The thesis cites an analysis of approximately 380,000 PyPI packages, in which each package had, on average, 2.6 direct dependencies and 129.6 transitive, non-unique dependencies. Reuse makes development faster, but it also means that a local change can propagate far beyond the repository where it originated.

Software evolution therefore has two directions. Reactive adaptation responds to external changes, such as a third-party library upgrade. Proactive improvement changes the system internally through bug fixing, refactoring, or feature development. Both directions create the same reliability question: how can we change software without losing control of its behavior?

I model this process in three phases. First, the system must perceive its environment and identify the need for evolution. Second, it must locate and modify the relevant logic. Third, it must deliver the evolved artifacts, including documentation that accurately communicates the new behavior.

[Timing] 0:50–2:20

[Sources]
- PhD thesis, Chapter 1, Section 1.1 Motivation.
- Figure: Figures/Chapter1/dependency.pdf.

As models grow richer, symbolic interfaces matter more
textPreview: THESIS / RELIABILITY GAP | As models grow richer, symbolic interfaces matter more

RICH MODELS

SYMBOLIC INTERFACES

FORMAL CHECKS

textPreview: RICH MODELS | preserve context and generate candidate changes. | SYMBOLIC INTERFACES | let people specify and inspect expectations. | FOR...

name: Footer Placeholder 3
text: College of Computing and Data Science
textPreview: College of Computing and Data Science

text:
Large language models have transformed software evolution. They can interpret natural-language requirements, generate code, explore repositories, and update documentation. These capabilities reduce the manual burden of maintenance and make increasingly autonomous evolution possible.

However, capability is not the same as reliability. A plausible generated answer is not a correctness guarantee. In software engineering, an answer that is almost right can still introduce a vulnerability, modify the wrong location, or communicate an invalid interface contract.

Jun Sun's 2026 article offers a useful way to frame the role of symbolic methods. As learned models preserve richer representations, explicit symbolic reasoning may become less central to the model's internal computation. Yet symbolic artifacts become more important at the human–AI boundary: specifications, contracts, invariants, explanations, and formal guarantees let bounded human users state expectations in forms they can inspect, revise, verify, and enforce.

This thesis operationalizes that interface idea for software evolution. Neural models handle ambiguity and semantic interpretation; executable evidence, program facts, Datalog rules, constraints, and formal checks make reliability expectations inspectable and testable.

[Timing] 2:20–3:50

[Sources]
- PhD thesis, Chapter 1, Section 1.1 Motivation.
- PhD thesis, Chapter 2, Sections 2.1–2.3.
- Jun Sun, "The Changing Role of Symbolic Methods in Artificial Intelligence," arXiv:2607.05168v1, 6 July 2026. https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.05168

text: College of Computing and Data Science
textPreview: College of Computing and Data Science

text:
The research question is: how can we combine empirical software data, large language models, and formal reasoning to improve reliability across the software evolution lifecycle?

I will present the thesis through three core studies, aligned with the lifecycle rather than publication chronology. These are complementary reliability interfaces, not one empirically integrated end-to-end pipeline.

Section one is CompSuite. For environment perception, it turns difficult external evolution risks into executable evidence through reproducible client–library incompatibilities.

Section two is DataLoc. For logic implementation, it translates natural-language intent into inspectable Datalog so that a deterministic engine can perform repository-scale structural inference.

Section three is MPChecker. For artifact delivery, it makes documentation and implementation comparable through extracted constraints, symbolic execution, fuzzy constraint logic, and SMT solving.

The studies use different artifacts, but they follow one principle: when a result can be reproduced, represented, or formally checked, the language model should not be the final source of truth.

[Timing] 3:50–5:20

[Sources]
- PhD thesis, Chapter 1, Sections 1.1 Motivation and 1.2 Contributions.
- Figure: Figures/Chapter2/neurosymbolic_approaches.pdf.
- Jun Sun, "The Changing Role of Symbolic Methods in Artificial Intelligence," arXiv:2607.05168v1, 6 July 2026. https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.05168

text: 01 / COMPSUITE · PERCEIVE
textPreview: 01 / COMPSUITE · PERCEIVE

text:
A reliable evolutionary process must first know what can break. Library upgrades are an important but difficult example.

An upgrade may preserve every public method name and type signature while changing behavior. For example, a library function may return an empty string in one version and null in the next. One client may safely handle both values, while another triggers a null-pointer exception. The incompatibility is therefore behavioral and client-specific; it may not be visible through API comparison or compilation.

Existing datasets mainly capture defects internal to one project. Upgrade failures are harder to collect because they involve two independently evolving components, a particular dependency version pair, a specific environment, and a test that exposes the changed behavior.

Without reproducible examples, it is difficult to train or compare compatibility checkers, debugging methods, regression-test selection tools, or future AI repair systems.

[Section] 01 / COMPSUITE · PERCEIVE

[Timing] 5:40–6:45

[Sources]
- PhD thesis, Chapter 3, Section 3.2 Client-specific Upgrade Incompatibility.
- Figure: Figures/Chapter3/example.pdf.

CompSuite isolates one upgrade and one test
textPreview: 01 / COMPSUITE · METHOD | CompSuite isolates one upgrade and one test

name: Content Placeholder 2

one dependency version

textPreview: START | passing client at a fixed commit | CHANGE | one dependency version | VALIDATE | the same test now fails

name: Footer Placeholder 3
text: 01 / COMPSUITE · PERCEIVE
textPreview: 01 / COMPSUITE · PERCEIVE

text:
CompSuite turns upgrade failures into controlled experiments.

We first selected popular open-source Java clients that use Maven, because Maven provides standardized dependency declarations, compilation, and test execution. We retained projects only when a fixed base commit compiled successfully and all tests passed.

For each eligible client, we identified dependencies with newer versions available on Maven Central. We upgraded one library at a time and reran the client’s tests. This isolation is important: if several libraries were upgraded together, we could not attribute a failure to one dependency.

When a test changed from passing to failing, we treated it as a candidate incompatibility-revealing test. We then manually examined the failure report and execution behavior to verify that the upgrade was the cause. For every accepted client–library pair, we preserved the client commit, the old and new dependency versions, the revealing test, its submodule, and the exact test command.

We created two tagged states. The base state uses the compatible dependency and passes the test. The incompatible state differs only in the selected library version and fails the same test. CompRunner automates downloading, checkout, compilation, testing, upgrading, retesting, and log collection.

[Section] 01 / COMPSUITE · PERCEIVE

[Timing] 6:45–8:20

[Sources]
- PhD thesis, Chapter 3, Sections 3.3 Dataset Creation and 3.4.2 CompRunner.
- Figure: Figures/Chapter3/architecture.pdf.

text:
The final dataset contains 123 reproducible, real-world client–library pairs, drawn from 88 distinct clients and 104 libraries. Every accepted instance was manually validated. The key contribution is not only the number 123. It is the experimental contract attached to every instance: a known-good state, a single controlled dependency change, an incompatible state, and a developer-authored test that demonstrates the failure.

This supports several uses. Compatibility tools can measure whether they detect known upgrade failures. Regression-test selection techniques can check whether they select the revealing test. Debugging tools can try to identify the responsible library change. AI systems can be evaluated on diagnosis and repair while using a real executable test as the oracle.

CompSuite provides the empirical foundation of the thesis: it makes external evolution risk reproducible and measurable before AI reasoning begins.

[Section] 01 / COMPSUITE · PERCEIVE

[Timing] 8:20–9:45

[Sources]
- PhD thesis, Chapter 3, Sections 3.1 Introduction, 3.4 Dataset Usage, and 3.5 Application Scenarios.

LOGIC IMPLEMENTATION
How can we locate code without relying on naming hints?
Perceive  →  LOCATE  →  Verify

[Timing] 9:45–10:05

text: 02 / DATALOC · LOCATE

text:
Code localization maps a natural-language request to the relevant files, classes, functions, or logic blocks. It is a prerequisite for repair: if an agent edits the wrong location, even a well-generated patch is irrelevant or harmful.

Existing methods report strong performance on issue-based benchmarks. However, many issue descriptions contain file names, function names, stack traces, or code fragments. In my analysis of SWE-bench Lite, more than half of the issues explicitly mention identifying information associated with the ground-truth location.

I call this the Keyword Shortcut. A model may appear to understand repository structure while actually following lexical anchors.

Consider this query: “Find all functions that have more than 15 parameters and are not an __init__ method.” There is no target function name to search for. The system must inspect program structure, count parameters, apply a logical conjunction, and return every valid location.

[Section] 02 / DATALOC · LOCATE

[Timing] 10:05–11:10

[Sources]
- PhD thesis, Chapter 5, Sections 5.1 Introduction and 5.2 Motivating Example.
- Figure crop from Figures/Chapter5/architecture.pdf.

text:
To expose this reasoning gap, I introduce Keyword-Agnostic Logical Code Localization, or KA-LCL, and construct KA-LogicQuery.

The benchmark contains 25 representative query combinations applied across nine repositories, giving 225 query instances. The queries deliberately avoid target names and instead require structural conditions such as parameter counts, inheritance, or call relations. Candidate locations were consolidated and then independently verified by two authors, producing ground truth at file, module, and function level.

I also construct KA-LogicQuery-Neg, where the query constraints are intentionally modified so that no valid location exists. This tests whether a system can abstain instead of always returning a plausible top-n guess.

[Section] 02 / DATALOC · LOCATE

[Timing] 11:10–12:00

[Sources]
- PhD thesis, Chapter 5, Section 5.4.1.1 Benchmarks.

text: 02 / DATALOC · LOCATE
textPreview: 02 / DATALOC · LOCATE

text:
DataLoc addresses this problem through a neurosymbolic division of labor.

The first stage runs offline. A language frontend parses the repository and extracts program facts. For Python, these facts describe files, modules, classes, functions, variables, and source locations, as well as relations such as containment, inheritance, imports, calls, and references. The facts form a structured intermediate representation of the repository.

When a user submits a natural-language query, the LLM analyzes the intent and translates it into a Datalog program. For the example on the previous slide, the generated rule selects function-definition facts where the parameter count is greater than 15 and the function name is not __init__.

The program is executed by Soufflé, a high-performance Datalog engine. Instead of repeatedly sending large amounts of raw source code to the LLM, the engine performs the structural traversal over the fact base. The result is deterministic for a given fact set and Datalog rule, and the rule itself provides an inspectable explanation of why locations were selected.

This division narrows the LLM’s role to semantic interpretation and formal query synthesis, while a specialized engine performs repository-scale deduction.

[Section] 02 / DATALOC · LOCATE

[Timing] 12:00–13:40

[Sources]
- PhD thesis, Chapter 5, Sections 5.3.1 Program Facts Extraction and 5.3.2 Agentic Workflow.
- Figure: Figures/Chapter5/architecture.pdf.

textPreview: PARSE | gate malformed rules | DIAGNOSE | probe empty intermediate relations | VERIFY | check candidates against the request

name: Footer Placeholder 3
text: 02 / DATALOC · LOCATE
textPreview: 02 / DATALOC · LOCATE

text:
There is still an important neural–symbolic boundary: an LLM may generate invalid or over-constrained Datalog. DataLoc therefore uses a synthesize–check–refine loop.

First, parser-gated validation prevents malformed programs from reaching execution. Unambiguous errors, such as reserved-name collisions, are repaired conservatively; otherwise, parser diagnostics are returned to the LLM.

Second, DataLoc observes row counts for intermediate relations. If a relation is empty, small diagnostic mutations test whether the emptiness is fragile—possibly caused by one incorrect constraint—or stable under conservative relaxation. These mutations are probes, not patches; their results are never returned as final answers.

After execution, the agent retrieves candidate source snippets and verifies them against the original request. If the result is excessively broad, the query is refined. If no location satisfies a valid rule, the system can return no match rather than manufacturing a recommendation.

The inference is verifiable relative to the extracted facts and synthesized rule. End-to-end errors remain possible, but they become visible and testable rather than hidden inside free-form generation.

[Section] 02 / DATALOC · LOCATE

[Timing] 13:40–14:55

[Sources]
- PhD thesis, Chapter 5, Sections 5.3.2.2, 5.3.3, and 5.3.4.
- Figure: Figures/Chapter5/mutate.pdf.

text: 02 / DATALOC · LOCATE

text:
On KA-LogicQuery, DataLoc substantially outperforms embedding-based, pipeline-based, and agent-based baselines.

Using Qwen3-Max, DataLoc reaches 73.35 percent file-level precision. Its file-level Perfect Localization Rate is 48.44 percent. This strict metric requires the predicted set to exactly equal the ground truth, without either missing or extra locations.

At function level, DataLoc still achieves a Perfect Localization Rate of 38.27 percent. Every evaluated baseline falls to zero on this metric. This matters because a long recommendation list can obtain a hit while still leaving a developer or repair agent with substantial noise.

The negative benchmark reveals another distinction. Existing systems generally continue returning top-n candidates even when no location satisfies the query. DataLoc returns a correct no-match answer for more than 70 percent of negative queries. It is not yet perfect, but it demonstrates that formal execution creates a meaningful abstention mechanism.

I also evaluated DataLoc on 274 retained SWE-bench Lite instances. On this conventional, keyword-rich benchmark, DataLoc is competitive rather than universally superior. With Claude 3.5, file-level Acc@5 is 81.02 percent, while DataLoc returns only about two candidate locations per issue on average. The trade-off is a smaller, more precise result set rather than maximal top-k coverage.

[Section] 02 / DATALOC · LOCATE

[Timing] 14:55–16:35

[Sources]
- PhD thesis, Chapter 5, Section 5.4.3.1 Effectiveness for logic query.
- PhD thesis, Chapter 5, Section 5.4.3.2 Effectiveness for general issues.

The architecture also changes the cost profile. With Claude 3.5 on KA-LogicQuery, DataLoc averages 39.3 seconds and 16.2 thousand tokens per query. On SWE-bench Lite, it reaches 81.02 percent file-level Acc@5 while returning about two candidate locations per issue on average, reducing the amount of downstream code a repair system must inspect.

The ablation study helps explain why the feedback mechanisms matter. On the representative first-25-query ablation subset, Qwen3-Max function-level precision rises from 18.20 percent in the Base configuration, to 38.93 percent with validation and repair, and to 55.20 percent in the Full configuration with intermediate-rule feedback. The exact values matter because they show that each verification layer contributes incrementally within this ablation setting.

The broader result is not simply that Datalog is fast. It is that the model is assigned a narrower role: interpret intent, synthesize a formal query, and verify candidates. Repetitive repository-scale traversal is assigned to a specialized engine.

This contribution therefore exposes a benchmark bias, supplies a diagnostic benchmark, and demonstrates that explicit intermediate reasoning can improve precision, efficiency, inspectability, and the ability to abstain.

[Section] 02 / DATALOC · LOCATE

[Timing] 16:35–17:55

[Sources]

DataLoc narrows the search to the logic that should change. Yet even a correct code change can be delivered with an incorrect public contract. The third core study, MPChecker, asks whether documentation still agrees with implementation.

[Timing] 17:55–18:15

[Sources]
- PhD thesis, Chapter 4, Sections 4.1–4.2.

text:
03 / MPCHECKER · PROBLEM
Documentation describes cross-parameter contracts
textPreview: 03 / MPCHECKER · PROBLEM | Documentation describes cross-parameter contracts

name: Content Placeholder 2

RELATIONSHIPS

SEMANTIC DRIFT

BLIND SPOT

textPreview: RELATIONSHIPS | one parameter changes the valid range of another. | SEMANTIC DRIFT | code and documentation can diverge silently. | BLIND...

name: Footer Placeholder 3
text: 03 / MPCHECKER · VERIFY
textPreview: 03 / MPCHECKER · VERIFY

text:
Finding and modifying the correct code is still not the end of evolution. A patch may be behaviorally correct while public documentation continues to describe the old contract. That mismatch increases misuse risk for future users and AI agents that rely on the documentation.

This problem is especially consequential in data-science and machine-learning libraries. Their APIs often expose many parameters whose valid values depend on one another. A constraint may say that one parameter is only used when another strategy is selected, or that a matrix must be absent when an input array is absent. These are logical relationships among several parameters, not independent range checks.

Existing inconsistency detectors largely focus on single-parameter properties such as names, types, nullness, or ranges. Multi-parameter constraints are harder because documentation uses diverse language, Python behavior is dynamic, and the corresponding condition may be distributed across several execution paths.

MPChecker treats this as a comparison between two representations: the constraint described by documentation and the constraint enforced by code.

text:
MPChecker has three phases.

The first is preprocessing. It parses Python files, separates code from documentation, supports common NumPy and Google docstring styles, and retains parameter descriptions likely to contain cross-parameter relationships. Unsupported constructs are rewritten into forms that symbolic execution can handle while attempting to preserve path constraints.

The second phase extracts constraints from both sides. For documentation, an LLM identifies constraint-related sentences and converts them into a restricted logical-expression format. The prompt defines permitted operators, uses decomposition, and includes few-shot examples. For code, dynamic symbolic execution explores feasible paths and obtains path conditions over input parameters. Z3 generates values for unexplored paths, while complex external calls or unsupported values may be abstracted to control path explosion.

The third phase compares the two sides. MPChecker asks whether a documented constraint is satisfiable and logically compatible with the code paths.

A crisp comparison would be brittle because the LLM may produce an almost-correct expression, such as a misspelled parameter or a slightly wrong operator. MPChecker therefore introduces fuzzy constraint logic and then checks the resulting compatibility using the SMT-based reasoner.

text:
The role of fuzzy logic is easy to misunderstand, so I want to make the boundary explicit.

The program semantics are not made fuzzy. Code execution paths remain crisp symbolic constraints. Fuzziness models uncertainty in documentation-derived constraints, including ambiguity in the text and errors introduced during LLM extraction.

The membership function compares atomic expressions through parameter names, values, and relational operators. Constraint-tree similarity is then composed through logical structure such as negation, conjunction, and disjunction.

This boundary layer tolerates small extraction errors without allowing the LLM to make the final consistency decision. The final decision uses SMT-based satisfiability and equivalence checking. In other words, uncertainty is modeled where it is introduced, while the decision remains formally grounded.

text:
I evaluated documentation extraction on 72 real constraints collected from scikit-learn, SciPy, NumPy, and pandas. MPChecker correctly extracted 66, giving an accuracy of 91.7 percent. The prompt components were important: without few-shot examples, accuracy fell to 62.5 percent, and without chain-of-thought, it fell to 79.2 percent.

For inconsistency detection, I generated 216 mutation cases based on eight patterns derived from resolved GitHub issues. Manual and SMT validation showed that 126 were genuinely inconsistent and 90 remained consistent.

The full MPChecker detected 117 of the 126 inconsistent constraints, giving 92.8 percent recall and 94.9 percent overall accuracy. The version without fuzzy words and fuzzy constraint logic achieved 69 percent recall, so fuzzy words and fuzzy constraint logic together contributed a gain of 23.8 percentage points. A raw LLM comparison of documentation and code achieved only 5.6 percent recall, while giving the LLM pre-extracted constraints improved recall to 41.3 percent. These comparisons indicate that the gain comes from the hybrid analysis design, not from asking a stronger prompt to judge the artifacts directly.

I also applied MPChecker to real library versions and reported 14 candidate issues across scikit-learn, Keras, Statsmodels, and Dask. Eleven were confirmed, and ten had been resolved at writing time: seven through documentation changes and three through changes to both documentation and code.

One example came from scikit-learn’s lars_path. The documentation stated that if X was None, the Gram matrix had to be specified. The code enforced the opposite relationship. After the report, the documentation was corrected to state that if X is None, Gram must also be None.

The paper’s contribution is therefore an end-to-end multi-parameter inconsistency checker with a customized fuzzy constraint layer and developer-confirmed real-world impact. MPChecker identifies a logical disagreement; it does not automatically declare which artifact is correct. Maintainers still determine whether code or documentation represents the intended contract.

textPreview: SYNTHESIS / ONE RELIABILITY ARCHITECTURE

text:
Across the three core studies, the intermediate artifact changes—from a test, to a Datalog rule, to a logical constraint—but the reliability pattern remains the same: make the model’s output executable, inspectable, or checkable.

CompSuite converts an external change into a reproducible pair of executions and a test oracle. DataLoc converts a natural-language localization request into program facts and an inspectable Datalog rule. MPChecker converts natural-language and implementation behavior into comparable constraint expressions.

These intermediate representations are the connective tissue of the thesis. A test case, a Datalog program, or a constraint expression is more useful for reliability than an unsupported natural-language answer because it can be rerun, inspected, or checked.

The work also shows that neural and symbolic components should not be treated as competitors. Neural models handle ambiguity and semantic translation. Formal artifacts support structural traversal, satisfiability analysis, and reproducible verification. The architecture determines which component is allowed to make which decision.

The thesis does not claim to have built one end-to-end autonomous maintenance system. It establishes datasets, benchmarks, tools, and design evidence for making such systems more dependable across the lifecycle.

textPreview: SYNTHESIS / BOUNDARIES & FUTURE WORK

text:
There are several important limitations.

CompSuite focuses on Java projects using Maven. It upgrades one dependency at a time, relies on existing tests as behavioral oracles, and is tied to fixed historical project and dependency versions. It therefore captures only failures exercised by the selected test suites and environments.

DataLoc has so far been evaluated only on Python. KA-LogicQuery contains 25 representative query combinations across nine projects; it is a diagnostic benchmark, not a complete model of every maintenance request. The deterministic engine does not by itself validate fact extraction or query translation, so either source of error can still produce an incorrect answer.

MPChecker currently focuses on Python data-science libraries and two major docstring styles. Python symbolic execution remains incomplete, particularly for new language features, external calls, strings, and complex objects. Its similarity threshold is heuristic, and a reported inconsistency does not determine whether code or documentation is the intended source of truth.

These boundaries motivate four directions: end-to-end benchmarks for AI-assisted self-healing under dependency evolution; automated repair of code–documentation inconsistencies; additional language frontends and richer program facts; and a verifiable intermediate language that bridges human intent and generated code before implementation begins.

text:
I began with a one-line dependency upgrade. Conceptually, the three core studies address successive reliability challenges around such evolution, although they are evaluated as separate contributions.

CompSuite makes an external failure reproducible. DataLoc gives an AI system a structured way to find relevant logic without depending on a lucky keyword. MPChecker checks whether delivered documentation agrees with the evolved implementation.

Together, these contributions support one conclusion: reliable AI-assisted software evolution should not depend on choosing between flexible intelligence and formal rigor. It should assign each of them the role it performs best.

Large language models provide adaptability, natural-language understanding, and generative power. Reproducible evidence and symbolic reasoning provide constraints, traceability, and verification. Their synthesis offers a practical path toward autonomous maintenance systems that are not only capable of changing software, but also able to justify and validate those changes.

That is the central contribution of this dissertation: a lifecycle-oriented foundation for software evolution that is intelligent where ambiguity is unavoidable and rigorous where correctness matters.

Thank you. I welcome your questions.
